sections.b: Nehemiah's memoir opens at Susa, where the king's cupbearer hears of Jerusalem's broken walls, weeps, fasts and prays (Nehemiah 1). Four months later he risks the king's displeasure by showing his grief, prays silently, and asks to be sent to rebuild "the city that holds my ancestors' graves" (Nehemiah 2:3). He arrives with royal letters and an escort, inspects the walls secretly by night, and rallies the people. Against mockery, threats and plots by Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, he organizes the whole community, builders with swords at their sides, and the wall is finished in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 3–6). In the middle of the work he confronts Jewish nobles who were enslaving their poorer brothers, cancels their claims under oath, and describes his own refusal of the governor's allowance (Nehemiah 5). He closes this part of his story by guarding the city and taking up the old register of the returnees to repopulate Jerusalem (Nehemiah 7).
sections.refs: Nehemiah 1:1–11; Nehemiah 2:1–20; Nehemiah 4:9; Nehemiah 4:14; Nehemiah 5:1–19; Nehemiah 6:3; Nehemiah 6:15; Nehemiah 7:1–5

common: Nehemiah is remembered as a man of prayer and action who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls in fifty-two days.
Christian books on leadership often use Nehemiah 1–6 as a model of vision, planning and perseverance.
uncommon: The Talmud faults Nehemiah for self-praise and for speaking badly of earlier governors, and says that is why the book was not named for him (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b).
Some scholars read the memoir as a self-defense addressed to critics in Judah or at the Persian court, whose claims should be weighed rather than simply accepted.
Some scholars have argued from Nehemiah 1:11 and Nehemiah 6:11 that he was a eunuch; others, such as Yamauchi, find the evidence weak.

claude.title: Claude's theory: a memoir written for an audience of One
claude.body: My own reading: the "remember me" prayers (Nehemiah 5:19; Nehemiah 6:14) are not interruptions but the frame. Nehemiah writes as if presenting his account to God, the only judge whose verdict he wants, and that explains both his frankness about his enemies and his habit of listing his own good deeds. The idea that the memoir resembles votive or memorial inscriptions set before a god was argued by Mowinckel and von Rad (see Williamson's survey), and Kellermann read it as an accused man's prayer; my addition is that the prayers in Nehemiah 4:4–5 and Nehemiah 6:14 make the same appeal for his enemies, so that the whole memoir reads as a case laid before a court.

sections.h: Mockery, plots and an open letter (Nehemiah 2–6)
sections.b: Sanballat and Tobiah are displeased as soon as Nehemiah arrives "to seek good for the Israelites" (Nehemiah 2:10). With Geshem they mock the builders and ask, "Are you in revolt against the king?" (Nehemiah 2:19), the charge that had stopped the walls before (Ezra 4:12–16). Sanballat jeers before the army of Samaria and Tobiah jokes that a fox could topple the wall (Nehemiah 4:1–3). When the gaps close they plot an attack with the Arabs, Ammonites and Ashdodites (Nehemiah 4:7–8). Then they target Nehemiah himself: four invitations to meet at Ono, an open letter accusing him of planning to be king, and a prophet hired to frighten him into the sanctuary (Nehemiah 6:1–14). Tobiah also keeps a network of letters with Judah's nobles, many bound to him by oath and marriage (Nehemiah 6:17–19). The memoir presents all this as opposition to God's work; historians add that the three men were neighboring rulers with real political and economic interests in Jerusalem.

common: Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem are usually remembered simply as enemies of God's people.
uncommon: Many historians see them as established leaders of neighboring provinces who resisted a rival power center, not as opponents of the LORD as such; Sanballat's and Tobiah's families gave their children names honoring the LORD.

sections.h: Sanballat of Samaria and the wall
sections.b: Sanballat, governor of Samaria, leads the opposition to Nehemiah's wall (Nehemiah 2:10; Nehemiah 4:1–2; Nehemiah 6:1–14). He speaks "in front of his brothers and the army of Samaria" (Nehemiah 4:2), and Nehemiah tells him and his allies, "you have no share in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 2:20). Sanballat's sons had names honoring the LORD, and an Elephantine letter of 407 BC shows the Jews of Egypt appealing to them for help. Nehemiah's exclusion of Samaria's leaders, and later his expulsion of the high priest's grandson who married Sanballat's daughter (Nehemiah 13:28), are often seen as steps toward the separation of Jews and Samaritans, whose temple on Mount Gerizim was built later in the Persian or early Greek period.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 2:10; Nehemiah 2:20; Nehemiah 4:1–2; Nehemiah 6:1–14; Nehemiah 13:28; John 4:9

sections.h: A Jew at the court of Artaxerxes
sections.b: Nehemiah gives a rare inside view of the Persian court: the winter palace at Susa (Nehemiah 1:1), the king's cupbearer and the danger of a sad face before the king (Nehemiah 2:1–2), the queen at a private meal (Nehemiah 2:6), letters for safe passage through the province Beyond the River and for timber from the king's park (Nehemiah 2:7–8), an armed escort (Nehemiah 2:9), and the royal tax that drove Judah's farmers into debt (Nehemiah 5:4). His opponents also fear what the king will hear (Nehemiah 6:6–7). The memoir shows a Jewish official who served a foreign empire loyally and used its power for his own people, while giving the credit to "my God's good hand" (Nehemiah 2:8).
sections.refs: Nehemiah 1:1; Nehemiah 1:11; Nehemiah 2:1–9; Nehemiah 5:4; Nehemiah 5:14–15; Nehemiah 6:6–7

sections.b: Nehemiah asks about "the Jews who had escaped, the ones left from the captivity" (Nehemiah 1:2), using the prophets' two words for the people saved through judgment. The report is that this remnant is "badly off and treated with scorn" (Nehemiah 1:3). The book that follows shows the remnant rebuilt: a walled city, a people enrolled by family (Nehemiah 7), and a community bound by covenant (Nehemiah 10).

Nehemiah is a book of prayer. Its long prayer of confession (Nehemiah 1:5–11) is built from Deuteronomy and Solomon's prayer: it praises the God who keeps covenant (Deuteronomy 7:9), confesses "I and my father's family have sinned," reminds God of Moses' promise to gather the scattered (Deuteronomy 30:1–5), and asks for success before the king. Then come short prayers in the middle of action: a silent prayer before answering the king (Nehemiah 2:4), a prayer for judgment on mockers (Nehemiah 4:4–5), prayer joined with posting a guard (Nehemiah 4:9), "make my hands strong" (Nehemiah 6:9), and the "remember me" prayers (Nehemiah 5:19; Nehemiah 13:14; Nehemiah 13:22; Nehemiah 13:31), two of them "My God, remember me for good" (Nehemiah 5:19; Nehemiah 13:31), with their dark twin, "remember Tobiah and Sanballat" (Nehemiah 6:14). Readers have praised the habit of turning to God in every situation; some have been troubled by the prayers against enemies and the requests for reward.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 1:4–11; Nehemiah 2:4; Nehemiah 4:4–5; Nehemiah 4:9; Nehemiah 5:19; Nehemiah 6:9; Nehemiah 6:14

common: Nehemiah's silent prayer before the king (Nehemiah 2:4) is often taught as a model of short, instant prayer.
uncommon: Some scholars think the "remember me" prayers mean the whole memoir was written as an offering laid before God in the Temple.

sections.b: Nehemiah prays "day and night, for the Israelites, your servants," and confesses sins he did not personally commit: "I and my father's family have sinned" (Nehemiah 1:6). Like Moses after the golden calf, he appeals to God's own act of redemption (Nehemiah 1:10; Deuteronomy 9:26–29), and like Daniel and Ezra he stands with the people rather than above them (Daniel 9:4–19; Ezra 9:6–15).

sections.h: The law in Nehemiah's prayer and reforms
sections.b: Nehemiah confesses that Israel did not keep "the commands, the rules and the rulings that you commanded your servant Moses" (Nehemiah 1:7), and grounds his hope in Moses' word of scattering and gathering (Nehemiah 1:8–9; Deuteronomy 30:1–5). In the debt crisis he does not quote the law, but his reform applies its heart: no interest or pledges against a poor brother, the fear of God, the redemption of kin sold into slavery, and the return of land (Nehemiah 5:7–11; Leviticus 25:35–43; Deuteronomy 15:1–18).

In 445 BC Jerusalem's wall still lay breached and its gates burned (Nehemiah 1:3), and the city was a "disgrace" before its neighbors (Nehemiah 2:17). Nehemiah inspected the southern walls by night (Nehemiah 2:12–15) and organized the rebuilding by sections, from the Sheep Gate around to the Sheep Gate (Nehemiah 3), naming gates, towers and pools that let us map the Persian-period city: the Valley Gate, the Dung Gate, the Spring Gate, the Pool of Shelah, the Water Gate, the Horse Gate, the Broad Wall and the towers of the Hundred and of Hananel. The wall was finished on the 25th of Elul, in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). Even so the city inside was large and nearly empty (Nehemiah 7:4). Archaeologists agree that Persian Jerusalem was small, centered on the City of David and the Temple mount; they debate whether any surviving wall is Nehemiah's.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 1:3; Nehemiah 2:12–17; Nehemiah 3:1–32; Nehemiah 6:15; Nehemiah 7:1–4; Jeremiah 31:38; Zechariah 14:10

sections.b: When Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem mock the builders, Nehemiah answers, "you have no share in Jerusalem, no rightful claim and no memorial there" (Nehemiah 2:20). All three were outsiders to Judah's community, though Sanballat and Tobiah worshiped the LORD and had family ties in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 6:17–19). Tobiah is "the Ammonite" (Nehemiah 2:10), and an Ammonite was barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:3–6, a law Nehemiah later enforces (Nehemiah 13:1–9). Readers differ on whether Nehemiah's line was a needed protection for a fragile community or a hardening of boundaries against neighbors who shared its faith.
sections.refs: Nehemiah 2:10; Nehemiah 2:20; Nehemiah 6:17–19; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Nehemiah 13:1–9; Ezra 4:3

sections.b: In the middle of the wall-building a great cry rises from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews (Nehemiah 5:1). Families need grain; farmers have mortgaged their land in a famine; others have borrowed to pay the king's tax; and daughters have been handed over as slaves (Nehemiah 5:2–5). The poor appeal to kinship: "We are made of the same flesh as our brothers" (Nehemiah 5:5). Nehemiah takes their side against the nobles and deputies, calls a great assembly, and has the land and interest returned under oath (Nehemiah 5:6–13). The chapter is one of the Bible's clearest pictures of a leader hearing the cry of the poor, the cry the law says God himself hears (Exodus 22:27).

common: Nehemiah 5 is often cited as a biblical model for social and economic justice.
uncommon: Some historians argue that Persian taxation, not local greed, was the main cause of the crisis, and that Nehemiah's reform shifted blame to Judah's elite while protecting the empire's revenue.

sections.b: Nehemiah charges the nobles and deputies, "You are lending on pledge, each of you against his own brother!" (Nehemiah 5:7). The Hebrew massa' may mean interest or the pledges taken as security; either way it broke the spirit of Leviticus 25:36, "Do not take interest or profit from him. Fear your God." Nehemiah demands the return of fields, vineyards, olive groves and houses, and of "the hundredth part" charged on silver, grain, wine and oil, probably interest of one percent a month (Nehemiah 5:11). He admits that his own household had been lending too, and proposes "let us drop this lending on pledge" (Nehemiah 5:10). The release is sealed by an oath before the priests and an acted curse (Nehemiah 5:12–13). The people later pledge to forgo the collection of debts every seventh year (Nehemiah 10:31).
sections.refs: Nehemiah 5:7–13; Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 15:1–3; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Deuteronomy 24:10–13; Nehemiah 10:31

sections.b: Nehemiah's reform in 5:11 does what the seventh-year release and the Jubilee were meant to do, returning land to its families and freeing the poor from debt (Deuteronomy 15:1–2; Leviticus 25:10; Leviticus 25:41), but it does not wait for a set year. Unlike the release in Zedekiah's day, which the owners quickly broke (Jeremiah 34:8–22), Nehemiah binds his with an oath and a curse (Nehemiah 5:12–13).

The poor of Judah say, "we are handing over our sons and daughters to be slaves. Some of our daughters are slaves already" (Nehemiah 5:5). Nehemiah contrasts this with the Jews abroad who have bought back their brothers sold to foreigners (Nehemiah 5:8; Leviticus 25:47–49). The law allowed an Israelite to serve for debt, but not as a slave: "They must not be sold the way a slave is sold" (Leviticus 25:42). Nehemiah's reform stops the selling; the text does not say whether the daughters already sold were freed.

Nehemiah says, "We have done what we could to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to the nations" (Nehemiah 5:8). This is the kinsman's duty of Leviticus 25:47–49, carried out by the community abroad for Jews sold to foreigners. The scandal of Nehemiah 5 is that Jews at home were selling the very brothers others were redeeming.

Many Christian interpreters count Daniel's seventy "weeks" (Daniel 9:24–27) from the permission Artaxerxes gave Nehemiah in his twentieth year, usually dated 445 BC (444 on Hoehner's count) (Nehemiah 2:1–8). Julius Africanus began this count about AD 220; Robert Anderson (1881) and Harold Hoehner (1977) worked it out with 360-day years to reach Christ's entry into Jerusalem. Others count from Ezra's commission in Artaxerxes' seventh year (Ezra 7) or from Cyrus, whose decree concerns the Temple (Ezra 1:1–4) though Isaiah says he will rebuild the city (Isaiah 44:28), and many take the numbers symbolically. Most critical scholars read Daniel 9 as written about 165 BC, counting from Jeremiah's prophecy to the crisis under Antiochus IV, with no reference to Nehemiah. The rabbinic chronology Seder Olam and Rashi count 490 years from the First Temple's destruction to the Second's; on ordinary dates that span (586 BC to AD 70) is 656 years, but Seder Olam gives the Persian period only 34 years. Nehemiah itself never mentions Daniel.

common: Many evangelical readers count Daniel's 69 weeks from Nehemiah 2:1 to the triumphal entry or the crucifixion.
uncommon: Most critical scholars hold that Daniel's seventy weeks end in the 160s BC and have nothing to do with Nehemiah's commission.

sections.b: To repopulate Jerusalem, Nehemiah gathers the people to be listed in the family registers and finds "the family register of those who had come up first" (Nehemiah 7:5). He copies it in full (Nehemiah 7:6–73), nearly the same list as Ezra 2, with about twenty differing numbers and several differing names. Both lists give the same total of 42,360, though neither list's parts add up to it. The repetition ties the walled city to the first return and shows how much belonging mattered in Persian Judah.

Nehemiah sees no miracles, yet he credits every success to God: the king grants his requests "for my God's good hand was on me" (Nehemiah 2:8; Nehemiah 2:18); God "wrecked" the enemies' plan (Nehemiah 4:15); the nations know "it was our God who had made this work happen" (Nehemiah 6:16); and "My God laid it on my heart" to enroll the people (Nehemiah 7:5; compare Nehemiah 2:12). God works through a king's mood, a governor's planning and a people's labor.

sections.b: Nehemiah's prayer quotes God's promise to gather the scattered and bring them "to the place I have chosen to make my name live there" (Nehemiah 1:9), joining Deuteronomy 30:4 to Deuteronomy's language for the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12:11). For Nehemiah the chosen place is Jerusalem, and rebuilding its walls is part of keeping that promise.

Nehemiah 6 shows prophecy used as a weapon. Sanballat claims Nehemiah has appointed prophets to proclaim "A king in Judah!" (Nehemiah 6:7); Shemaiah, a prophet paid by Tobiah and Sanballat, urges Nehemiah to hide in the sanctuary (Nehemiah 6:10–13); and Noadiah the prophetess and other prophets try to frighten him (Nehemiah 6:14). Nehemiah tests Shemaiah's word by God's law: a word that calls for sin cannot be from God (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:20–22).

Facing a threatened attack, Nehemiah uses the words of Israel's holy wars: "Do not fear them! Remember the Lord, the great and fearsome one, and fight for your brothers" (Nehemiah 4:14; Deuteronomy 7:21; Deuteronomy 20:3–4), and "Our God will fight for us" (Nehemiah 4:20; Exodus 14:14). Yet no battle is fought: God frustrates the plan (Nehemiah 4:15), and the people build with weapons ready.

sections.h: A layman barred from the sanctuary
sections.b: Shemaiah urges Nehemiah to hide "inside the sanctuary" (Nehemiah 6:10), the hekhal or Holy Place, which only priests could enter (Numbers 18:7). Nehemiah refuses: "who like me could go into the sanctuary and stay alive?" (Nehemiah 6:11). The scene shows how seriously the Second Temple's holiness was kept even by its greatest lay leader.
